issues.item: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: The self-blame item is not clinically supported elsewhere in the profile. There are no Negative Appraisal or Memory items indicating guilt, responsibility, shame, or a trauma narrative that would make repeated self-blame coherent. With this formulation, the only strong cycle is Threat ↔ Maladaptive Strategies, so maladaptive strategies should plausibly function to manage current danger/safety concerns. Drug use and avoiding thinking fit that threat-management loop, but repeated self-blame instead implies an unrepresented negative-appraisal process and sits weakly with the rest of the selected items.

vignette:
Dara is a 31-year-old Cambodian American man who works as a carpenter and lives with his wife. When he describes the night that continues to stay with him, he does not tell it as a distant story. He returns to details that still feel immediate: the hard glare of police lights, the confusion of being shouted at before he understood what was happening, the abruptness of hands on his body, the sense that once he was on the ground he could not control anything that happened next. He had been outside after work, still in his work clothes, tired and dusty, when officers approached him aggressively. He remembers trying to answer, trying to keep up with rapid commands, and then being forced down. What has stayed with him most is not a single blow or sentence but the experience of being trapped in full view of other people, unable to predict what the officers would do from one second to the next. He came away from it with the conviction that danger can arrive without warning and that once it begins, no one slows down long enough to hear him.

In the weeks afterward, Dara found that his mind kept circling back to the incident even when he did not want to think about it. He would replay what he had said, whether he moved the wrong way, whether he should have kept quieter, spoken sooner, looked less frightened. He repeatedly blames himself for what happened, returning again and again to the idea that if he had handled those few minutes differently, the police would not have turned on him. His wife has heard variations of the same question late at night—why did I do that, why didn’t I just stay still, why didn’t I know what they wanted? Even when she tells him that what happened was not his fault, he continues to go over it as if there must be some mistake he can still locate and fix.

At the same time, he works hard not to think about the event at all. He has become skilled at cutting off conversations, changing the subject, and keeping himself occupied with tasks that leave no room for reflection. On job sites he throws himself into measuring, sanding, carrying, anything concrete and physical. If an image from that night starts to come up, he tries to push it away before it forms fully. He sometimes uses drugs to blunt himself further, especially on evenings when the thoughts feel close and he is afraid of where his mind will go if he lets it settle. He does not describe this as wanting to get high so much as wanting to get out from under his own head for a while.

His sense of danger now extends far beyond encounters with police. In any room, Dara looks first for the wall. At restaurants, waiting areas, even at family gatherings, he feels unsafe unless his back is against a solid surface and he can see the whole room. If someone suggests a seat in the middle, he becomes tense and distracted, scanning movements around him rather than listening. He says he knows other people do not understand why this matters so much, but for him being unable to see who is coming or where someone is standing feels intolerable. At work this shows up in small but noticeable ways. In clients’ homes he positions himself carefully, often choosing spots where no one can approach from behind. If a homeowner or contractor steps unexpectedly into his space while he is bent over a cabinet or framing, his body stiffens immediately.

He is also on edge when anything takes longer than expected. If his wife is late coming home, if a text goes unanswered, if a supervisor disappears for longer than planned on a job, his mind jumps quickly to the sense that something bad is happening. Waiting has become especially difficult because it resembles the worst moments of the police encounter, when he did not know what was about to happen next and every second seemed to hold threat. He can sit in his own living room and still feel unable to relax, even when he tells himself he is safe. His body remains taut, his attention fixed outward, as if safety is temporary and can be revoked without notice.

Over months, these habits have narrowed his life. His wife has grown frustrated and worried about how often he seems mentally elsewhere, either stuck in self-accusation or shutting down any mention of what happened. He has become harder to be with in ordinary situations that require waiting, flexibility, or trust. He finally agreed to seek help after an argument at home that began with something small—his wife running late—and escalated because he was certain something had gone wrong and could not calm himself even after she walked through the door unharmed. By the time he came in, Dara was exhausted by the constant vigilance and ashamed of his drug use, but he was also afraid that if he stopped staying on guard, stopped replaying his own mistakes, or let himself think directly about that night, he would be left exposed again in the same helpless way. What he hopes for, cautiously, is not to forget what happened, but to be able to sit in a room, wait for someone he loves, and feel like the danger is not already on its way.
